transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I... my mom made the appointment, I think. I just, I don't really know how to explain it because there's not really anything happening, it's more like nothing is happening at all. Mostly I just can't make myself do anything anymore. I just sit in my room. And it's not like I'm doing anything in there, I just sit on the edge of the bed or in the chair by the window, usually with the exact same clothes on that I wore the day before, and the day before that, and probably the day before that too. 

I used to do things, you know? I had all this yarn, I used to knit these thick scarves, and I had this whole stack of notebooks where I would journal every single night, color-coded and everything. I even used to go walking around the neighborhood for hours just to get fresh air and look at the trees. But now... the yarn is just sitting in a plastic bin gathering dust, and I haven't opened a notebook in I don't even know how long. I look at them and it's like there's a huge, heavy wall between me and actually doing it. And my mom, she comes upstairs and knocks on the door and she keeps asking me what is wrong and why I am just sitting there and what is going on with me. And I hear her, I really do, but I barely even have the energy to open my mouth to answer her. It just takes way too much effort to push the words out of my throat, so I just stare at the wall instead. It's just... everything is just too heavy to move.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

No... no, I don't think so. It's actually just really, really quiet in my room. Like, almost too quiet, you know? Because I'm just sitting there for hours and hours, so I end up hearing every little normal thing in the house. I hear the air conditioner kicking on through the vent right above my closet, and it makes this low rattling sound that never really stops. And I can hear the cars going by on the street outside, especially when it rains and the tires make that hissing noise on the wet pavement. 

And my mom, I hear her downstairs all the time. I can hear her slippers on the hardwood floor, just shuffling back and forth between the kitchen and the living room, and the TV murmuring in the background when she turns on her shows in the evening. But it's just regular stuff like that. There aren't any voices talking to me or anything out of the ordinary. It's mostly just... silence. Just this huge, empty silence that fills up the whole room and presses down on me while I'm looking at the wall. Sometimes the quiet is so thick it kind of makes my ears ring, just a high-pitched whine from absolutely nothing happening, but nobody is talking to me when they aren't there. It's just me in there. Just me and the quiet.
Do you believe something unusual or disturbing is true about you or the world, even when other people tell you it isn’t?

Well, I... I mean, my mom tells me I'm wrong about this, but she doesn't see what I see. She doesn't read the emails the way I do. It started back when I was still trying to take those college classes, before I just stopped going and started sitting in my room all day. I was trying to get into the healthcare program, doing the clinic practicum stuff, and... well, they didn't want me there. I know they didn't. 

It wasn't like they came out and said "we don't want you," because they can't do that, right? They have rules. So they did it through the school portal. Every time they sent an email or left a comment on one of my assignments, they would change the wording just a tiny bit. Like, they wouldn't use standard phrasing. They would use these specific, little altered words, and I realized it was a code. They were marking me. They were using those little wording changes to flag me in the system as someone who shouldn't be allowed to work in healthcare. 

I tried to show my mom. I printed out all the emails and the assignment rubrics and I highlighted the words—like how one professor said "ensure careful attention" instead of just "pay attention," or how the practicum coordinator kept using the word "monitor" in this really specific way. I laid them all out on the kitchen table to show her the pattern, how it was this whole coordinated thing between the professors and the clinic people to push me out. But she just sighed and told me they were just regular messages. She said I was reading too much into it and that professors just talk like that. But she doesn't get it. She doesn't understand that they have to do it that way so they don't get sued, but they still have to make sure the other people in the program know I'm marked. Even now that I'm not going to classes, I know the mark is still there in the portal. They made sure of it.
Have there been times when you believed the school was marking you even when you were not feeling depressed?

Well, I... I don't really think it works like that. It's not about being depressed. Because the emails were there before I stopped doing things, and they're still there now while I'm just sitting in my room. It's not like the mark in the portal goes away just because I'm sitting on the edge of my bed all day, you know? 

I remember when I first noticed it, I was actually doing okay. I was still knitting those scarves, I was still writing in my notebooks every night, using my different colored pens. I was going to my classes and getting my assignments done. I was just sitting at my desk, looking at my laptop, and I saw that first email from the practicum coordinator. The one where she used the word "monitor." And I just knew. I knew right then what they were doing. It didn't matter how I was feeling, it was just right there on the screen in black and white. And then the next week, the professor used that phrase, "ensure careful attention," and I started printing them all out. 

So it's not... it's not a mood thing. It's not because I'm heavy and tired now. The school did what they did, and they coordinated the whole thing, and that's just a fact of what happened. I could be out walking around the neighborhood looking at the trees like I used to, and it wouldn't change the fact that they coded those messages to flag me in the system. The mark is just there. It doesn't care if I'm happy or sad or just staring at the wall.
When you talk, do other people ever tell you that your thoughts or speech are hard to follow or seem jumbled?

No, no one says that. I mean, my mom doesn't say that, and she's the only one I really talk to anymore. When I talk to her, I'm just telling her what I need, like if I want a glass of water or if I need her to pick up a different kind of soap from the store because the one she bought last time had a weird smell that made my head hurt. I explain it to her very clearly. I tell her exactly what I mean, from the beginning of the thought to the end. I don't jump around or get confused. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to explain to her why I couldn't eat the sandwich she made, because the bread was cut diagonally instead of straight across, and I explained the whole reason, step by step, about how the diagonal cut makes the corners too sharp and it changes the way the bread feels when you hold it. I went through the whole explanation, and she understood me perfectly. She just sighed and made another one. She never says my words are jumbled. She might not agree with me, like about the emails from the school and the way they marked me, but she never says she can't follow what I'm saying. I use all the right words. I make sure I do. I think about the words before I say them, and I put them in a line, like beads on a string, just one after the other so they make a perfect sentence. So, no, nobody tells me I'm hard to follow. They just... they just don't want to listen sometimes. But that's different. That's not because my words are wrong.
Have you ever had a time when you felt so energized or unusually up that you needed much less sleep than usual?

No, I... I don't think so. I don't get energized like that. It's actually the exact opposite, really. I don't have times where I feel "up" or like I don't need to sleep. Sleep is... well, I sleep a lot. Or I try to, anyway. I mean, I spend most of my time in my room now, like I said before. I'm usually just sitting on the edge of my bed, and my limbs feel so heavy, like they're filled with wet sand or lead or something. I don't have this... this bursting energy to go do things or run around. 

I usually go to bed at like 9:30 or 10 o'clock every night because there's just nothing else to do, and I turn off the main overhead light, but I always leave the little desk lamp on because it casts this softer shadow against the closet door, and I just pull the heavy quilt up and wait to fall asleep. I definitely need my sleep. If I don't get it, my head feels all fuzzy and thick. So I never feel like I can just skip it or like I only need a couple of hours. 

My mom actually gets frustrated with me because she thinks I sleep too much or that I'm just lying around all day, which I am, but it's not because I'm energized or awake. It's just... I'm just heavy. Even when I was still doing my notebooks and knitting the scarves, I still slept normal hours. I've never had a time where my body just didn't want to sleep. I don't even know what that would feel like, to be honest. I just feel tired.
Do you feel sad or depressed most days?

No, I do not think sad is the right word. I mean, sad is when... when you drop something you really like or when a dog dies in a movie, right? That is sad. You cry when you are sad. I do not cry. I have not cried in... I do not even know how long it has been since I actually shed a tear. I just sit there. 

Like I was saying before about my bed, I just sit on the edge of the mattress. It has a blue fitted sheet, the one with the little white anchors on it that my mom bought at the store a few years ago because she thought it looked nautical and fresh. I just sit on those anchors and stare at the closet door. But I am not crying while I do it. I am not feeling heartbroken or miserable or anything like that. I think people always assume that if you are in your room all day you must be weeping into your pillow, but my pillow is completely dry. I make sure it is perfectly flat every morning against the headboard, right in the center. 

So, no, not depressed. Depressed sounds like a dark rain cloud, always sighing and feeling sorry for yourself. I do not feel sorry for myself. I just feel... well, I do not really feel much of anything emotionally. It is just that heaviness in my arms and my legs that I mentioned before. Like the wet sand. It is just a physical weight, pulling me down into the mattress, making it hard to even walk to the kitchen to get the water my mom leaves out for me on the counter next to the sink. But it is not a sad weight. It is just a completely empty weight. So I do not think depressed is right at all. I am just here. I am just existing in the room.
Do things that used to feel enjoyable to you, like knitting or journaling, still feel enjoyable now?

No, they don't. I mean, I don't even do them at all anymore, so I wouldn't know if they feel enjoyable, but just looking at them doesn't make me feel anything. I have this wicker basket in the corner of my room, right next to the closet door I was telling you about, and it's completely full of yarn. There's this really thick, chunky mustard-yellow yarn right on top that I bought specifically to make a winter scarf, and the knitting needles are just sticking right out of the center of the skein. They are size ten needles, the bamboo kind, because I always preferred those since they don't click as loud and sharp as the metal ones do. But I haven't touched them in... I don't even know. Months, probably. I just look at the basket from the bed. It doesn't look fun. It just looks like an impossible amount of work. 

And it is the exact same thing with my journaling. I have these black composition notebooks, the standard ones with the black and white marble pattern on the front cover, stacked perfectly on my desk. I used to write in them every single day, filling up the pages from the very top margin all the way to the bottom edge with blue ink. But now the pen is just sitting on top of the stack, and I don't write a single word. I don't knit, I don't journal, I don't even go for my walks around the neighborhood like I used to do in the late afternoons when the sun was starting to go down and it wasn't so bright. 

Mostly I just... I just can't make myself do anything anymore. Nothing at all. I just sit in my room on the anchors on my bed. And I don't even change my clothes. I've been wearing this same oversized gray t-shirt—the one with the faded college logo on it—and these soft black sweatpants with the frayed drawstring for... I think four days now? Maybe five. It just doesn't seem to matter if I change them, because putting on clean clothes takes a lot of steps, and I'm not going anywhere anyway. 

My mom will come in to bring me that water, and she sees me just sitting there, not knitting, not writing, wearing the exact same clothes as yesterday and the day before, and she gets this pinched, worried look around her mouth. She'll stand in the doorway and ask me, "What's wrong? Why aren't you doing your hobbies?" But I... I barely have the energy to answer her. It takes so much effort just to push the air out of my lungs to make a sound, let alone explain that I just don't care about the yarn or the notebooks anymore. I just stare at her, or I maybe mumble that I'm fine, because actually trying to form a real sentence about why I'm not doing anything is just too exhausting. It's just all too much effort.
Have there been times when, for at least two weeks, you felt depressed or lost interest in almost everything most of the day, nearly every day?

I don't really know about two weeks, or keeping track of time like that. My mom has this big glossy calendar in the kitchen, the kind with a different picture of a bird for every month—I think this month is a blue jay, or maybe a cardinal, I can't remember—but I don't go out there to look at it anyway. So I don't know if it's been exactly two weeks or four weeks or what. The days just sort of blur together into one long, continuous thing. 

And like I was saying before, I really wouldn't use the word depressed. I know you're asking about that again, but it's just not the right word. Depressed people are sad. I'm not sad. I'm just empty. And as for losing interest... well, yes, I don't care about the yarn or the notebooks anymore, but it's not like it's some little two-week phase I'm going through. It's just how every day is now. 

The light comes through my window blinds—they're those cheap white plastic ones that get kind of brittle and yellowed from the sun—and it makes these long, thin stripes across the beige carpet. And I just sit on my bed on those blue anchors and watch those stripes slowly move across the floor, from the edge of the closet door over to the wicker basket, until the sun goes down and the room gets dark. That's the whole day. Nearly every day, just like you said. But I couldn't tell you how many weeks it's been happening. It feels like the stripes have been doing that forever. So I don't really have a specific two-week time to tell you about, because it's just... it's just my life right now. I don't measure it in weeks.
For at least one month, have you been convinced that the school was marking you in those emails?

I don't know if I'd say "convinced" like it's just some idea I came up with out of nowhere. It's just what's happening. And yes, it's definitely been longer than a month. It's been about two months now that it's been this... this set in stone. 

It started right around the time the weather started getting colder, when the frost first started showing up on the grass in the mornings outside my window. That's when I first noticed the pattern in the school portal. The way the login screen would glitch just for a second, and then the practicum emails started coming in. They always have these specific subject lines, like "Practicum Requirements Update" or "Clinical Placement Review," but the capitalization is always slightly off. Like, the 'R' in Review will be italicized, or there will be a double space after the word Placement. That's how they mark me. That's how I know the email is specifically meant to track me, to let me know that they are watching my account and marking my progress, but not in a good way. 

And it's been exactly like this, this fixed and constant, for the past two months. Every time I open my laptop—which is this heavy silver one my mom got me for graduation, it has a little dent on the left corner from when I bumped it against the desk—I see the emails sitting there in my inbox. I don't even open them anymore. I just look at the subject lines, at the double spaces and the weird italics, and I know they are marking me. It's not a feeling or a suspicion. It's just a fact. For two whole months, every single day, just sitting there in my inbox, marking me.
During a time when you were not having that emptiness and loss of interest, did you still believe the school was marking you?

I... I don't really know how to answer that. A time when I wasn't having the emptiness? I mean, like I was just saying about the window blinds and the stripes on the carpet, this is just... it's just my life right now. I don't even really remember what it felt like before the emptiness started, or if there even was a 'before' recently. It feels like this heavy, thick blanket that just covers everything in my room, from the wicker basket full of mustard-yellow yarn to the desk with the black composition notebooks. 

And the emails... well, the emails with the weird italics and the double spaces, they've been there for two months, ever since the frost first started showing up on the grass outside my window. But the emptiness? I don't know when that started. Did it start before the frost? After the frost? I don't keep track of the days on that glossy bird calendar in the kitchen, so I can't just draw a line for you and say, oh, here is where the emptiness stopped and the emails continued. They just... they're both just here. 

The heavy silver laptop sits on the desk with the dented corner, and the emails are inside it marking me, and I sit on the bed on the blue anchors, and I'm empty. I can't separate them for you. I don't know if there was a time when one was happening and the other wasn't, because it's all just happening right now, all together, every single day. I just look at the laptop, and I look at the floor, and it's all exactly the same. So I really don't know what to tell you about a time without the emptiness, because I just don't have a time like that to look back at. I don't know.
Before you started believing the school was marking you, was there ever a time when you lost interest in almost everything?

I... I don't know. Like I said, I don't really have a timeline for any of this. The emptiness, the loss of interest... it's all just this big blur. I mean, before the emails started marking me, back before the frost was on the grass and I noticed the weird italics in the subject lines... was I empty then? Did I care about things then? 

I know I used to care about the yarn. I had this whole project planned out, a blanket made entirely of mustard-yellow squares, and I had all these black composition notebooks filled with the patterns and the stitch counts. I would sit on my bed—the one with the blue anchors on the sheets—and I would just knit for hours, listening to the cars drive by outside my window. But then the yarn just started looking like... nothing. Just dead strings in a wicker basket. And the notebooks just looked like trash. 

But when did that happen? Was it before I noticed the practicum emails on my heavy silver laptop? Was it after? I honestly can't tell you. My mom's bird calendar in the kitchen doesn't help because I never look at it, and the days just bleed into each other. The sun comes up, the light makes those stripes through the cheap plastic blinds, the stripes move across the beige carpet, the sun goes down. That's it. That's the only way I measure time now. So I can't tell you if the emptiness came first, or if the emails came first, or if they both just sort of swallowed me up at the exact same time. I just don't know. I can't untangle it all.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you believed the school was marking you, but you were not feeling empty or uninterested in everything?

I feel like you keep asking me the exact same thing just... just using different words, and I really don't have a different answer to give you. Two weeks? I mean, two weeks is just fourteen days, right? Fourteen times the sun comes up and pushes those light stripes through the cheap plastic blinds and across the beige carpet. But I don't count them. I don't sit there and mark off fourteen little squares on my mom's glossy bird calendar in the kitchen. 

So if you're asking me to perfectly slice out a two-week chunk of time where I was absolutely sure about the practicum emails—you know, the ones with the weird italics and the double spaces on my heavy silver laptop—but I somehow wasn't feeling like a completely hollowed-out shell... I just can't do it. I can't separate them like that. It’s not like I have this neat little diary where I wrote down, oh, today the school is marking me, but I feel totally fine and I really want to knit with my mustard-yellow yarn. It doesn't work like that. 

The laptop is sitting right there on the desk with the dented corner, and the wicker basket of dead yarn is on the floor, and I'm on the bed with the blue anchors, and it's all just... it's all just one big heavy thing that sits on top of me. I can't tell you if there were fourteen days of the emails happening without the emptiness happening too, because it's all just a blur of the exact same day repeating over and over. I really just don't know how to give you the exact timeline you're looking for.
Before you ever noticed the school emails seemed coded, had there already been a period when you no longer enjoyed things like knitting or journaling?

I... I really, really don't know how else to explain this to you. You're asking me about 'before' again, before the emails, before the coding, before the italics and the double spaces. But I just... I don't have a 'before' that I can see clearly anymore. It's like trying to look through a window that's completely frosted over, you know? Like the grass outside my window in the mornings, just completely covered in this thick, white frost where you can't even tell what color the grass underneath is supposed to be. 

Before I noticed the practicum emails on my heavy silver laptop... was I already not enjoying the knitting? Was the mustard-yellow yarn already just sitting there in the wicker basket, doing nothing? Were the black composition notebooks already shoved to the side on the desk with the dented corner? I don't know. I honestly don't know. Because when I try to think back, when I try to picture myself sitting on the bed with the blue anchors and actually wanting to knit, actually wanting to write down stitch counts... it feels like I'm trying to remember someone else's life. 

I don't know if the emptiness swallowed me up first, and then I started seeing what the school was doing, or if I saw what the school was doing and then the emptiness came. It's not like my mom's glossy bird calendar in the kitchen where you can just flip back a page and say, 'Oh, look, October 12th, stopped liking yarn. November 3rd, noticed the coded emails.' It doesn't work like that. It's all just mashed together in my head. The stripes of light through the cheap plastic blinds, the beige carpet, the dead yarn, the heavy laptop, the emails... it's all just one big, heavy, confusing mess, and I can't pick it apart for you. I just can't. I'm sorry, but I really just don't know the order of any of it.
Have there been days when you felt deeply hopeless?

Hopeless? I... I don't think hopeless is the right word. Hopeless implies that you were actually hoping for something in the first place, right? Like, to feel hopeless, you have to have some kind of picture in your head of how things are supposed to be, and then feel devastated when they aren't that way. Like back when I was planning out that blanket, I had all the stitch counts in my black composition notebooks, and I hoped it would turn out perfectly square. If I messed up a row, maybe I'd feel frustrated. But hopeless? No, I don't think I feel hopeless. 

Because to feel deeply hopeless, you have to actually feel something deep, and I just... I don't. I don't sit on my bed with the blue anchors and cry about the future. I don't cry at all. It's not a sad feeling. It's not this crushing despair where I'm wishing things were different. It's just... flat. It's just the stripes of light moving across the beige carpet, from the window with the cheap plastic blinds, over and over. Hopeless is too big of an emotion. It takes energy to be hopeless, I think. You have to care that things are bad to feel hopeless about them. 

I just watch the dust motes float in the air when the sun hits the room. The heavy silver laptop sits on the desk with the dented corner, and the dead strings of mustard-yellow yarn sit in the wicker basket, and I just exist in the middle of it. I don't look at my mom's glossy bird calendar and feel hopeless about tomorrow, because tomorrow is just going to be another day of the sun moving the shadows around the room. There's no hope, but there's no hopelessness either. It's just... nothing. So no, I wouldn't say I've had days where I felt deeply hopeless. I don't have big feelings like that anymore.
For at least two weeks, have you had the belief that the school was marking you during a time when you were not feeling this empty and unable to enjoy things?

I... I really, really don't understand why you keep asking me to chop time into these little two-week pieces. It's like you're trying to cut a cake with a butter knife that's completely dull. I just told you, I can't separate the emptiness from everything else. But... but if you're asking about the school marking me, yes, I've had that belief. I mean, it's not a belief, it's just what's happening. 

Since I was in those college classes, before I dropped out, I've known what they were doing. It started on the school portal. I'd log in on my heavy silver laptop, the one sitting right there on the desk with the dented corner, and I'd see the assignment comments. And then it was the clinic practicum people. They were sending these emails, and it wasn't just regular text. It was the little wording changes, you know? Like they'd use a specific word instead of another, or they'd put an extra space between two words, or use italics in a way that didn't make any grammatical sense. 

It was a code. They were using those little wording changes in the emails and the assignment comments to mark me. They were marking me as someone they don't want in healthcare. They were signaling to each other that I shouldn't be there. And my mom... she stands in the kitchen by her glossy bird calendar, and she looks over my shoulder at the screen, and she says, 'Honey, they're just regular messages. They're just telling you about the schedule.' But she doesn't see it. She doesn't see how the words are arranged. She just sees the surface, like looking at the frost on the grass and not knowing what's underneath. 

But I know. I know they've been marking me since I was in those classes. I just... I can't tell you if there was a perfect fourteen-day window where I knew they were marking me but I also wanted to pick up the mustard-yellow yarn and knit. Because the emails and the portal and the heavy feeling... it's all just sitting on me at the same time. I can't pull them apart for you. I know they're marking me, but I don't know the exact dates, and I don't know how to make you understand that the timeline doesn't matter when it's all just happening constantly.
Have you been eating much less than usual lately?

Eating less? I... no, I don't think so. I don't think I'm eating any less than I usually do. It's not like I'm hungry, exactly, but I'm not avoiding food either. 

My mom is always in the kitchen anyway, standing right by that glossy bird calendar—I think it's on the page with the cardinal right now, or maybe the blue jay, I don't really look at the birds anymore, just the shiny paper when the light hits it. But she's always in there, and she makes the meals. She'll bring a plate into my room, or she'll call me out to the table, and I just eat it. Like yesterday, she made this chicken soup with those tiny, star-shaped noodles. I just sat at the table and watched the metal spoon go into the bowl, and then into my mouth, and then back into the bowl. Over and over. It's just a mechanical thing, you know? Like the clock ticking on the wall or the stripes of light moving across the beige carpet. 

I don't skip meals because my mom wouldn't let me anyway. She's always hovering around, asking if I want a turkey sandwich, asking if I want a glass of orange juice. And I just say yes, or I just take the plate she hands me, because it's easier than trying to explain that I don't care. It takes way too much energy to argue about a sandwich. So I just eat it. I chew the bread, and it's just texture in my mouth. It doesn't taste good, it doesn't taste bad, it's just... matter. It just goes into my stomach and sits there, heavy, like the laptop on the desk. 

So the plates are still getting emptied. The food still goes away. I'm eating the same amount I always have, I guess. It's just another thing that happens during the day while I'm sitting there. So no, I haven't noticed eating less.
Lately, have other people noticed that you move or speak much more slowly than usual?

Move or speak slowly? I... no, nobody has said that. I mean, who else is there to even notice besides my mom? And she hasn't said anything about me moving in slow motion or anything like that. 

She complains sometimes that I'm not doing *enough*, that I'm just sitting on the bed with the blue anchors all day, but that's not the same as moving slowly. That's just not moving at all. When I actually do get up—like if I have to go to the bathroom, or if she calls me into the kitchen to eat one of those turkey sandwiches—I just walk normally. I put my feet on the beige carpet, one after the other, and I walk at a regular speed. It's not like I'm wading through wet cement or molasses. It takes a perfectly normal amount of time to get from my bedroom door down the hall to where she's standing by that glossy bird calendar. I'm just walking.

And talking... well, you're listening to me right now. Am I talking slowly? I don't think I am. Sometimes I just don't want to talk, because it's exhausting. Like when my mom asks me a million questions about what I want to do today, or if I want to get out my mustard-yellow yarn, and I just look at her because I don't have an answer. But that's just me being quiet. When I actually open my mouth to say something, the words come out just like they always did. I don't drag out the syllables. I don't sound like a record playing on the wrong speed. I just... say the words. 

Like when I'm reading the assignment comments on my heavy silver laptop, I read them at a normal speed. I see the wording changes and the spaces just as fast as I ever did. I'm not slow. I'm just empty. There's a big difference between not having the energy to do things and actually doing things slowly. So no, my mom hasn't said anything about me moving or speaking slower, and I definitely haven't noticed it either.
Do you feel worthless?

Worthless? I... no. No, that's really not the right word at all. I don't think you're understanding what I mean when I say I'm empty. 

Worthless implies that there's a value to be measured, you know? Like you have a value, and it happens to be zero, or it's negative. It means you feel bad about yourself, like you're broken or a burden or something. But I don't feel bad about myself. I don't sit on my bed with the blue anchors and think, "Oh, I'm a terrible person, I have no worth." I just don't have anything inside me to feel terrible *with*. 

It's like... think about a glass in the kitchen. If my mom leaves a glass sitting on the counter, right under that glossy bird calendar, and there's no water in it, you don't look at it and say the glass is worthless. You just say it's empty. It's just glass and air. It's just existing in the space it takes up. That's what I'm doing. I'm just existing on the beige carpet, taking up space. It doesn't mean I'm worthless. 

Even with the school, and the clinic practicum people. Yes, they're marking me. I know they are. I see the codes on my heavy silver laptop, the extra spaces and the weird italics in the assignment comments.
